records.title: Show HN: WallHop – 12ft.io is gone, so I built a replacement
records.author: TheWaffleHax
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Josh. WallHop is a free paywall bypass: paste an article URL (or prefix any URL with wallhop.io/) and you get the readable article without the paywall popup, ads or clutter. No signup, no extension.

I built it after 12ft.io went away. The News Media Alliance took it down in July 2025 and I missed having something I could hit from my phone.

How it works: it started as a fork of everywall/ladder (GPL-3.0) and I've modified it heavily since. Instead of relying on one trick, it chains several bypass methods per request and falls back to archive.is when they all fail, so one site blocking one technique doesn't break it.

Things that might be interesting:

- iOS Shortcut: on iPhone, tap Share > WallHop from any article in Safari or another app. This is how I use it 95% of the time. - It works on Medium member-only posts, which 12ft never handled. - Bookmarklet for desktop, plus /raw/<url> and /api/<url> endpoints if you want to script it.

I've tested it against most major news outlets and a bunch of local papers. It won't work everywhere. There are SOME server-side paywalls that are out of reach, and I'd rather say that up front. If you find a site that breaks, I'd love the link, and I can likely figure out a way to bypass it!

records.title: Show HN: ManimGX – Manim's API on a Rust/wgpu engine, for 3D videos in Python
records.author: sinaatalay
records.storyText:
Video as code took off with the Opus 5.5 release. People now make videos by writing code, with Remotion, HyperFrames and others.

We wanted the same for 3D videos. You can use something like Blender, but it's heavy to install and slow to render.

So we made ManimGX:

- Lightweight: a 65–110 MB download, depending on the OS

- Easy to install: pip install manimgx (Python 3.13+), with no system dependencies

- Cross-platform: macOS, Windows and Linux, and even the browser via Pyodide and WebGPU

- Blazingly fast: a Rust + wgpu engine, 90.6× faster than Manim CE and 18.7× faster than Blender Workbench, from launch to finished MP4

- Compatible with Manim Community Edition's API, with LaTeX and Typst math built in

Now it's much easier for anyone with a coding agent to make 3D computer graphics videos.

Repo: https://github.com/academa-labs/manimgx

Docs: https://manimgx.academa.ai

X post: https://x.com/sinaatalay/status/2109045945149395421

Happy to answer any questions!

records.title: Show HN: My radio station calls its listeners
records.author: attels33
records.storyText:
I was driving, listening to European Hit Radio, the host hyping up the top 20, and thought, hmm, this is basically the same script every day. Could this be AI? I have some experience in voice AI, so I had the parts lying around. A few hours and several slop sessions later: Canarics Radio.

It ended up talk only news instead of music (for now, maybe AI music next?). Why - music royalties are the actual expensive part of radio. Two AI hosts discuss the day’s headlines in Latvian and English, 24/7. They know they’re AI and joke about it on air.

It’s cheap: about 1 euro a day per station in model calls. Not a lot of code either, about 400 lines of dependency free Node plus ffmpeg, but who reads code anymore, right? There is no streaming server: episodes are rendered to HLS chunks in a bucket, and the "live" playlist is a pure function of the wall clock. A stateless endpoint computes what’s playing "now", every listener hears the same thing, and if generation fails the wheel just loops. Silence is impossible.

The silly part: leave your phone number on the page and my voice agent calls you back, takes your question, and the hosts answer it in the next episode (Europe, US, CA, AU, NZ numbers).

Happy to answer questions about my music taste. Though as you already know I listen to EHR pop, the answer is: none.

records.title: Show HN: Aporium – A UMAP galaxy of 5800 philosophy excerpts in conversation
records.author: kevinjacobh
records.storyText:
The Starfield is Aporium’s 3d topic explorer made using the embeddings of 5800 philosophy excerpts styled to resemble a navigable galaxy. It utilizes UMAP for excerpt-placement and extracted excerpt metadata for thematic region labeling. Scroll adjusts zoom, right click pans, and left click orbits.

Aporium is my solo effort to bring the wisdom of the great works of philosophy into a format that balances depth of analysis, ease of reading, and multi-author perspective. I started this project 8 months ago to reduce my social media screen time, hoping to replace it with something addictive yet enriching.

By extracting short yet meaningful 2-8 sentence excerpts from public-domain works and generating their embeddings, I created a pipeline utilizing cosine similarity and AI judging to form synthetic conversation ‘threads’ of dialogue using the real writings of philosophers. Not AI-generated ‘what would this author have said on X topic’; their real words. A byproduct of these embeddings is the ability to create structured, explorable 3d maps with distinct regions of thought. This went on to become the Starfield linked above.

Here are a few representative examples of near-conversational sounding threads.

Francis Bacon on anger, Cicero in disagreement: https://www.aporium.app/thread/ex_248310dbc3aff2ceb529d093

Emerson on self-reliance, Marcus Aurelius in opposition: https://www.aporium.app/thread/ex_57ea1e2ac8cc9b6f493f57c1

Montaigne on lying, Nietzsche disagreeing: https://www.aporium.app/thread/ex_6d7c367d5530d3b3e0fa34b2

Thoreau on vanity, Pascal shifting emphasis: https://www.aporium.app/thread/ex_6b6f8b13fcfc0e50cbab1af0

My goal is to extract and link together in conversation the most impactful ideas and excerpts from humanity’s greatest works, creating separate corpora for poetry, theology, psychology, history, and more. Any feedback is much appreciated.

Lemme know what you think and please share any and all feedback!

That’s why we built guilds.run.

records.title: Show HN: A Safari extension to accelerate animated WebP images
records.author: 76SlashDolphin
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

The other day I had to do some work with a lot of large animated WebP files on my Macbook running Safari and noticed that it handles them very poorly. They load slowly and it seems like they're constantly being decoded, also with really poor performance. Here's a website with similar images to what I was working with: https://colinbendell.github.io/webperf/animated-gif-decode/w...

On that website, my M1 Macbook Air decodes the boat and smoke images at fewer than 5FPS, and the brown underwater office one has a constant stutter. The performance on my iPhone 15 Pro is very similar with the additional annoyance that I have to manually "Play" each animation.

This was one of those small things that bothered me during my work week so on the weekend I decided to see if I can do something about it. I started by experimenting with the decoder itself and noticed that if you decode a static WebP image it's pretty fast - approximately as fast as other browser engines. It's actually fast enough to fit in 0.16ms. So I thought "what if I just take the WebP animation decode the frames one by one with the internal decoder and just plonk them on a canvas" and after quickly vibe coding the experiment, the images on the test page played at 60FPS flawlessly.

So I reported the issue to Apple, and then made an extension that will find animated WebP images in webpages and swap them out for the same trick. Have a look here: https://github.com/IliaMManolov/safari-animated-webp-extensi...

It's currently GitHub-only and I've spent about a day on this all-in-all but I hope anyone that has to interact with similar images in the future finds it useful. Let me know if there's interest in this too, I'd happily put it on the App Store if I can somehow have the extension cover the developer fee.

records.title: Show HN: Mailbox Viewer – publish FOIA email dumps as a static Gmail-like site
records.author: rahimnathwani
records.storyText:
Responses to public-records (FOIA, or California PRA) requests often arrive as PST or mbox files, which 'normal' people don't know how to open. If they're lucky they can import them into Apple mail or the Outlook desktop client.

But it's hard to share with others, and impossible to link to a specific thread or a specific spot in a specific thread.

Jmail (https://jmail.world), the Gmail-style viewer for the Epstein emails, was heavily upvoted on HN, because it felt so easy to use. I had hoped the team would open source the code, but I don't think they did.

My first attempt at my own version (made for a specific pst file I received) was usable, but had some limitations. Recently, I threw Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) at the problem.

This is the result.

The mbv build command turns a mailbox (PST, mbox or Maildir) into:

- a set of parquet files

- a word index

- embeddings.

You upload those to any static host that support HTTP range requests (e.g. Cloudflare R2) and deploy one front-end viewer (e.g. Vercel) for any number of mailboxes. There's no backend computation. The browser queries the Parquet files with DuckDB-WASM over HTTP range requests.

It rebuilds conversations (including from Outlook's Thread-Index), keeps folders as labels, supports Gmail's search operators (from:, has:attachment, before:, OR, "phrases"), searches text inside PDF and Office attachments, and adds semantic search with a small embedding model that runs in the browser.

Every view has its own URL, so you can deep link to a search and a conversation. This link searches a school district mailbox for "straight white male" and opens the matching thread with the hits highlighted:

https://mail.ocaho.com/youcubed-2026-03#search/Straight%20wh...

Demo with a fictional mailbox: https://mail.ocaho.com/demo

Code (MIT): https://github.com/rahimnathwani/mailbox-viewer

records.title: Show HN: Throw Alice and Bob into Sagittarius A*
records.author: steve6390
records.storyText:
Black Hole Lab is an open source physics simulation of a rotating black hole and two observers, Alice and Bob. You can launch Alice and Bob on paths around or into the black hole and watch events play out. The simulation lets you see a slice of the physics with one or two dimensions of space plus one of time.

As a fun extra, Alice and Bob each have a beacon that can transmit a radio wave in all directions. The simulation calculates and shows the wavefront of these signals, accounting for the warping of space and time by the black hole. The simulation also records whenever Alice and Bob receive each other's transmission.

The simulation takes pains to respect Einstein's equations of general relativity. To the precision of the numerical integration, the effects shown in Black Hole Lab are really what the math of general relativity says will happen. Black Hole Lab specifically uses the Kerr metric, which is an exact solution to Einstein's equations of general relativity for a rotating mass. That said, physicists agree that general relativity cannot be the final word on black hole physics. Nobody can say what would really happen to Alice and Bob.

My original goal for black hole lab was to try to understand the strange time compression effects at the inner horizon, which physicists call infinite blueshift. IMHO, Black Hole Lab succeeds in showing this effect in an understandable way. I added a specific discussion of infinite blueshift in the readme.

records.title: Show HN: Flopper is a hardware explorer for AI infrastructure and beyond
records.author: triwats
records.storyText:
Hello!

I built Flopper to make it easier to compare GPUs and understand the tradeoffs for workloads for AI and beyond.

When researching GPUs from say Nvidia, AMD, and Huawei, I kept running into the same problem: specs were scattered across datasheets, and matching them to available configurations, vendors, and prices was cumbersome and a bit weird and frankly annoyingggg! AMD made me make an account :(

So I started a place to bring that information together.

Flopper lets you compare GPU specs, including TDP and compute throughput in terms of flops/tops, alongside estimates for AI workloads or other compute workloads (say, ~FP32 based) I recently added pricing data from dozens of providers to help track how prices change over time. Getting reliable quotes for systems like the NVL72 is still particularly difficult tbh, not sure how I can tell you how much that costs easily due to them being behind large procurement contracts and big multi-nationals.

One thing that's become fairlyyyy clear is the interest in consumer cards and local LLMs.

The bigger challenge is connecting advertised specs to real-world performance. In our testing so far, I’ve seen roughly 85% of advertised throughput, but that’s a ballpark observation for the workloads I’ve tested, not a general rule and so variable (power, cooling, workload etc).

I'm considering a CLI that lets people run benchmarks and submit results, potentially using MLPerf as an automation? That way, we can all compare quoted performance with the workload, configuration etc.

I'd love feedback: what information is missing, how can I improve it? And what would you need to see to trust a community-submitted benchmark?

Corrections and additions also very welcome - some of the measurements are best efforts (and simple multiplications) but I hope it's of some use.

Thanks for looking :)

records.title: Show HN: Running EmbeddingGemma2 on the Browser
records.author: glpcc
records.storyText:
During this summer I wanted to start a side project, and I got the idea of embedding image search directly on your browser. This wasn't a new idea for me as i had built it at work as a small internal tool for me to search the company icons semantically instead of scrolling in the company deck.

This week (October 2026) Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, which puts text, images, audio and video in the same vector space, so I moved the app over to it from the siglip2 model i was using before. The main differences I've seen, apart from video and audio support, are the multilingual capabilities, and the better understanding of long queries, although it still struggles with generic images being too "in the middle" of the embedding space and ranking high on unrelated searches.

I know small SaaS products like this are a tough sell these days. I built it anyway because I grew up learning to code by hand, reading about solo developers with crazy ideas shipping little products that made some side money, and I wanted to go through that whole process myself: build it, deploy it, and put it in front of people.

How it works:

The model runs in your browser, transformers.js, WebGPU or WASM, depending on your device. It does work on mobile, although image upload do take way too much there.

Your files and their vectors are stored on the server so collections sync across devices. I know this could be a privacy concern, but at least for me the ease of use is worth it.

For quantisation im using fp16 on desktop with capable GPUs and q4 on any other device.

The big caveat is that first visit downloads the model (about 170 MB, or about 520 MB on desktops with fast WebGPU), it's cached after that, but you do have to wait a bit.

You can try it for free without an account on the example collections. As a side not, i took the travel photos (the Photography collection, from Venice) and the flower photos myself. There’s a free tier if you want to upload your own files, and paid plans if you need more.

If you have this problem too, I hope this shows that searching your own files using embedding models is genuinely useful, whether you use this or build your own. And if you’d rather not build it, I’d be happy to have you as a user. Any feedback is very welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Korosta – Remember and highlight job postings you've seen
records.author: gocova
records.storyText:
# What is and whats not

Korosta is a privacy-first user-customizable tool to highlight job postings based on how frequent are those, and your ratings: * how often the job postings appeared to the user -> fade repeatedly seen job postings * learns from your ratings with a simple local model -> highlight relevant ones * 2 versions: free and pro * almost everything is kept local (ratings, recipes, customizations, history), only licensing and payments require a server * no account required to use it (just when doing the purchase)

This is not a job tracker, job board, or automated application system. It just annotates what you already have visible in your browser's tab.

## Links

chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/korosta/dhpnogbefak... firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/korosta/

Howto create recipes fast (With the help of a LLM): https://covatools.com/korosta/howtos/create-cookbook-with-an... Website (with ultra short videos): https://korosta.app

# Why

This idea started like 2 years ago, when I was laid off from a tech company (2024's common rounds), and I started the stressful job searching. For job searching, my main platform was, and still is, linkedin: I perfected my url parameters so I can easily have my 10 different tabs. But one questions that commonly had, was "Have I already seen this job post?", and honestly, I wont be saving manually every item in a tool like trello (or the new ones). That question plus my bad memory had me with: "that role is awesome!!! ohhh I already seen it... but 2 months ago" (something like job posting recycling? maybe).

The main objective of this tool/extension is to reduce the load / fatigue of remembering what you have already seen (and not in just a single site), and also highlight what could be interesting to you personally (by learning with your ratings) -> less time searching, and thus, giving more time to apply in the relevant ones, or doing something else (like recovering your energy).

One thing I also spent time around was in the customization / editor (+ the howto in the page), so almost anybody can extend the tool (recipes/cookbook) <- I get frustrated when I love a tool but I fully depend on the developer

# beyond the technical part (more context... you can skip it, and test already)

Around 16.5 years ago I wanted to develop and sell apps, like the trend in those days... I did not. One year ago, I was thinking the same with the first version, the tool was working (even though over engineered), but I got discouraged by myself by reading all the terms of services, legal + fiscal topics, all the things that I did not know... plus some sites are very aggressive with their terms of use and tools like this.

I got a job, then changed my career path to a contractor, and meanwhile I started looking for a job again, but since the end of 2025 I really understand the new difficulties of the job market + not being sooo young, so I took the previous tool, refurbished it but with a different mindset: customization first with a simple learning algorithm so it can highlight interesting jobs to the user -> the name of the tool "Korosta" means highlight in Finnish (its difficult to find a good name ha).

I do think that is even more relevant to release it now because of AI: some platforms are pushing heavily their AI-based search engines, that are not so easy yet to customize -> putting more stress / burden on us.

In terms of monetization, I defined it based on: I am not keen of subscriptions, I grew up with shareware (like Doom... you can guess my age now), and when a single payment give you something (I wont distribute this in floppies, though). And it ended like: pay once and keep for the same major version.

I learned a lot, and I am still learning, with this development, so I want to hear your comments. Also, If you are looking for a job right now, how does the extension feel to use?

records.title: Show HN: InfiniWord – infinite multiplayer word search
records.author: Static2280
records.storyText:
Hi everyone! I’ve been on leave since welcoming our first child into the world which has given me time, in between 3 am diaper changes and with the tireless support of Claude, to get to personal projects.

One of those is a game for my wife who’s big into word searches. Around the time she expressed interest in wanting a word search game I was reminded of “1 million chessboards” (https://eieio.games/blog/one-million-chessboards/) and thought that would be fun to replicate in this space. Thus was born infiniword - an infinite, persistent, procedurally generated, realtime multiplayer word search game.

Alongside the standard word search features, Infiniword has the following unique ones:

Scrabble like tile multipliers (currently a 1/2000 chance for a tile to be worth 3x)

First find bonuses for being the first to find a word globally

25 achievements of various difficulties

All time and weekly leaderboards across points, found words, and first finds

Simple friends list with the ability to teleport to them and hunt for words together

Shareable events like a specific word you found, winning a “wanted word”, placing in the top 3 of a “challenge zone”, and more.

“Wanted words” - a timed hunt for a specific word in a circular area that comes with a bonus based on how much time is left

“Challenge zones” - every 3 hours a random 100x100 tile zone becomes a “challenge area” where you compete with all other players to get the most points from words in the zone.

“Daily challenge zone” - same thing as the main world challenge zones but the world is just the 100x100 area with a new seed each day. Competition runs from 10am central US to 10 pm central US. The first daily launches here soon, go check it out! https://infiniword.com/daily

Hope everyone enjoys playing it as much as my family and I do!

records.title: Show HN: Wesnoth wouldn't run on my phone -- I rebuilt the combat in the browser
records.author: jdzikowski
records.storyText:
Hi, I'm Jakub and I used to dream to publish a novel before turning 40, but life is life -- yesterday was my 40th birthday and I'm publishing a game instead.

A few months ago I started experimenting with building a turn based tactics game with a combat system heavily inspired by the Battle for Wesnoth. The main reason was that I could not make Wesnoth work on my phone :D I iterated on it over and over, polishing graphics, finding background music, balancing units, and here it is. There is a fully playable skirmish mode -- 3 factions x 3 units x 3 levels. AI opponent, 4 difficulty levels, fog of war, time of day changing unit stats, various terrain types and traits (poison, healing, others). It runs in the browser and -- if you choose to sign in -- it syncs across devices. You can start on desktop and finish on mobile.

I wanted to make it casual, but also serious at the same time. For me many games are either too complex and require much time (like most of 4x) or too naive in terms of combat system or graphics (like many mobile games).

I'm developing campaigns -- I already have a rough scenario for the first campaign, and the first playable match (not released yet). My main focus is on single player game, while there is also a multiplayer in progress.

My goal was to make all game modes free and with no ads. There is a single paid feature -- verified play, which basically means we verify your games server side, so you can participate in future global ranks. I'm not sure if that's enough to cover costs, but we'll see.

I’m still a dev with a full-time job. Hexnoth is so far mostly a hobby project, and it's fulfilling in terms of artistic expression and storytelling. I won't create the next Baldur's Gate or Age of Wonders, but I feel great power and agency, and I can shape it nearly entirely the way I want. Or the way you'd like to have it -- just drop a message.

records.title: Show HN: An Agentic Virtual Machine
records.author: wikitopian
records.storyText:
I'm interested in feedback pertaining to the features in my agentic harness project.

* Addressable Memory

Everything in the context is divided into receipts with internal urls that the model can address, with a "pulled preview" approach where dozens of spammy tools can be streaming output at the same time without flooding the attention window.

* Perpetual Context

Plurnk has no compaction algorithm because the addressable memory empowers the model to curate its context on its own terms. This has an incredible impact over extended sessions, with the agent retaining its bearings for weeks on end.

* Model-Oriented Programming Language

Plurnk presents the model with a "virtual machine" that it "programs," with all core and extended tools having a common markdown-adjacent shape.

* First-Party Benchmarks

The architecture is basically sqlite+node, with the only dependency weight being ANTLR for building the programming language AST and the giant bag of wasm treesitters necessary for all of the integrated pattern dialect functionality (glob, regex, jsonpath, xpath, graph, fts).

My latest benchmark, published on the separate bench repo, is comparable with bare pi agent, despite all of these bells and whistles.

Looking for honest, including brutally honest, feedback. All MIT. No telemetry. Works on everything node can be installed on (tested on mac, android, arm64, etc).

Now some the details, already listed in my production readiness (https://docs.model-ship.ai/production-readiness/#production-...) plan:

- it has prometheus metrics and grafana dashboard

- can run under docker, k8s or simply native install

- automatically sizes model context

- has MCP support

Feedback would be much appreciated.

records.title: Show HN: LoRA over GGUF – Train Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in 40G VRAM
records.author: woctordho
records.storyText:
Open weight AI is like open source software. Users not only run the weights, but also modify the weights. It matters to develop training framework for local hardware.

The method to train large AI models on local hardware is generally called QLoRA (Low Rank Adaptation over Quantized base model). In the last few years it's usually done with HuggingFace Transformers (which is the basis of training frameworks such as Unsloth and Axolotl) and bnb 4-bit base model. However, bnb does not yet support MoE models, so the local training of recent MoE models seemed stall for some time.

Since Transformers 5.18, it's started to support GGUF, and it supports recent models with MoE and sparse attentions (and it's not slow, already faster than llama.cpp on Mac). GGUF is a versatile container format. It can be smaller than 4 bpw with surprisingly good quantization quality, so there are new possibilities for local training.

I've shown that we can train Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B-A6B + 51B engram) in 40 GiB VRAM without CPU offload. I've optimized it on Strix Halo and it trains at 200 token/s. There is still room to optimize, compared to > 1600 token/s prompt processing we've achieved, and the common sense that LoRA training (with gradient checkpointing) takes 4-5x work of prompt processing. CPU/disk offload (like Strata) and multi-GPU also need more work that I'm not currently focusing on.

On Strix Halo we can also train DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B-A13B) in 90 GiB VRAM at 100 token/s, but I think it's less practical than Qwen3.8FN for local use.
